story.title: Trump Appoints Stephen Miller as New Chief of Staff
story.summary: President Donald Trump has appointed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller, known for his hardline immigration policies, is expected to reinforce Trump's agenda following disappointing midterm election results. His promotion signals a commitment to the administration's controversial domestic policies.

explore_lenses.label: What changes on November 9?
explore_lenses.title: Miller takes over the White House staff
explore_lenses.summary: Trump announced that Stephen Miller will become White House chief of staff on Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles is leaving the post for the Trump Political Operation, rather than departing the president’s wider political orbit.

claims.text: Trump named Miller the 33rd White House chief of staff on November 6, succeeding Wiles.
Trump said Miller’s start date is November 9, 2026; Wiles said her White House chief-of-staff service ended November 6.

Congressional Research Service says presidents appoint some White House and Executive Office of the President personnel without Senate approval, unlike positions for which Congress has required advice and consent.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: Public reporting said it was unclear on November 6 whether Wiles’s deputies would remain in place, and no public announcement reviewed specifies who will assume Miller’s former policy and homeland-security responsibilities.

explore_lenses.label: Why does Miller’s promotion matter for policy?
explore_lenses.title: An immigration-policy aide gains broader control
explore_lenses.summary: Miller enters the job from a role spanning White House policy and homeland security, making immigration a central part of his record but not the only area he can influence as chief of staff. The position coordinates the president’s staff and agenda; it does not itself change immigration law or automatically create a new policy.

claims.text: The White House’s 2026 staff report listed Miller as assistant to the president, deputy chief of staff for policy, and homeland security adviser.

The administration’s January 20, 2025 immigration order directed agencies to use lawful means to enforce immigration laws against inadmissible and removable noncitizens and encouraged agreements allowing qualified state and local officers to perform specified immigration functions under federal supervision.
The White House described Miller as a driving force behind the administration’s border-security agenda; that is the administration’s characterization of his role and its claimed results.
Forecast: Republican strategist Barrett Marson told Axios that the choice signaled Trump was unlikely to adopt a conciliatory posture after the midterms.

explore_lenses.label: What do supporters and critics say?
explore_lenses.title: Backers cite execution; Democrats promise resistance
explore_lenses.summary: Administration allies portray Miller as an experienced implementer of Trump’s agenda. Democratic leaders characterize the move as evidence that Trump is not moderating after the midterms and say they will use congressional oversight and litigation to oppose policies they attribute to Miller.

claims.text: Vice President JD Vance called Miller an “amazing patriot,” while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he looked forward to working with Miller to advance the president’s agenda.
Former deputy chief of staff Taylor Budowich called Miller an organized and competent policy operator; this was included in the White House announcement compiling supportive reactions.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Trump “couldn’t have made a worse choice” and said Democratic congressional majorities would oppose him.
Rep. Robert Garcia said Oversight Democrats would continue investigating Miller and contesting his policies in Congress and the courts.

story_report.summary: President Donald Trump named Stephen Miller the 33rd White House chief of staff on Nov. 6, replacing Susie Wiles after Republicans’ poor midterm performance. Trump said Miller would begin Nov. 9, while Wiles said her service ended Nov. 6. The change elevates an official known for his role in Trump’s immigration policies and puts him in charge of the White House staff operation, though successors for his previous policy and homeland-security duties have not been announced.

sections.heading: Miller’s Previous White House Portfolio
sections.body: The White House’s 2026 staff report listed Miller as assistant to the president, deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser. The administration’s January 2025 immigration order directed agencies to enforce immigration laws against inadmissible and removable noncitizens through lawful means and encouraged agreements allowing qualified state and local officers to carry out specified federal immigration functions under supervision. The White House has characterized Miller as a driving force behind its border-security agenda.

sections.heading: Miller Appointment Draws Split Reaction
sections.body: Vice President JD Vance called Miller an “amazing patriot,” and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he looked forward to working with him to advance the president’s agenda. Former deputy chief of staff Taylor Budowich described Miller as an organized and competent policy operator. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Trump “couldn’t have made a worse choice,” while Rep. Robert Garcia said Oversight Democrats would continue investigating Miller and challenging his policies in Congress and the courts.

unresolved.text: It was unclear in public reporting whether Wiles’s deputies would remain in place, and no reviewed public announcement identified who would assume Miller’s former policy and homeland-security responsibilities.
The specific immigration, domestic-policy and staffing decisions Miller will prioritize as chief of staff remain unresolved.
The practical scope of congressional oversight will depend on committee priorities, requests for testimony or records, and any executive-privilege assertions.

related_stories.title: Jay Rockefeller, Former Governor and Senator, Passes Away at 89
related_stories.summary: Jay Rockefeller, the last member of his family's political dynasty, has died at the age of 89. He served as the governor of West Virginia and was a longtime U.S. senator, known for his advocacy on healthcare, education, and working families' needs. Rockefeller was born into a prominent family and forged a significant political career.

related_stories.title: Momentum Builds for Coalition Talks in Israel as Eisenkot Gains Support
related_stories.summary: Following inconclusive elections, opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot is gaining momentum in his efforts to form a government in Israel. He has received significant backing, including from Arab parties, as President Isaac Herzog prepares to announce who will be tasked with forming the new government. Eisenkot aims to replace long-serving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

related_stories.title: ANC Faces Significant Decline in South African Local Elections
related_stories.summary: The African National Congress (ANC) is projected to receive less than a third of the vote in South Africa's local elections, marking a significant decline from previous years. With over 80% of ballots counted, the ANC is on track for its worst-ever election performance, estimated at around 32%. This decline is attributed to widespread voter dissatisfaction over issues such as water outages and power cuts, leading to potential coalition challenges in major cities like Johannesburg and Tshwane.

related_stories.title: New Zealand General Election Results Leave Parliament Divided
related_stories.summary: The New Zealand general election has concluded without a clear winner, resulting in a highly divided parliament. Preliminary results show the two main parties nearly deadlocked in the popular vote, leading to expectations of extended coalition negotiations. Minor parties, including the Opportunity Party, may play a crucial role in forming a government.
